claim: Embryonic taste bud primordia are specified as taste placodes on the tongue surface.
source: Embryonic taste bud primordia are specified as taste placodes on the tongue surface and differentiate into the first taste receptor cells (TRCs) at birth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background statement about taste bud development.

claim: Taste placodes differentiate into the first taste receptor cells (TRCs) at birth.
source: Embryonic taste bud primordia are specified as taste placodes on the tongue surface and differentiate into the first taste receptor cells (TRCs) at birth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background statement about taste bud development.

claim: Throughout adult life, TRCs are continually regenerated from epithelial progenitors.
source: Throughout adult life, TRCs are continually regenerated from epithelial progenitors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about adult taste cell renewal.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling regulates TRC development and renewal.
source: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling regulates TRC development and renewal, repressing taste fate embryonically, but promoting TRC differentiation in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge about SHH function.

claim: SHH represses taste fate embryonically.
source: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling regulates TRC development and renewal, repressing taste fate embryonically, but promoting TRC differentiation in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge about SHH function in embryos.

claim: SHH promotes TRC differentiation in adults.
source: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling regulates TRC development and renewal, repressing taste fate embryonically, but promoting TRC differentiation in adults.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge about SHH function in adults.

claim: TRC renewal initiates at birth.
source: Here, using mouse models, we show TRC renewal initiates at birth and coincides with onset of SHHs pro-taste function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The onset of TRC renewal coincides with onset of SHH's pro-taste function.
source: Here, using mouse models, we show TRC renewal initiates at birth and coincides with onset of SHHs pro-taste function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Foxa1 and Foxa2 are potential SHH target genes in lingual progenitors at birth.
source: Using transcriptional profiling to explore molecular regulators of renewal, we identified Foxa1 and Foxa2 as potential SHH target genes in lingual progenitors at birth and show that SHH overexpression in vivo alters FoxA1 and FoxA2 expression relevant to taste buds.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data and qPCR results shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: SHH overexpression in vivo alters FoxA1 and FoxA2 expression relevant to taste buds.
source: Using transcriptional profiling to explore molecular regulators of renewal, we identified Foxa1 and Foxa2 as potential SHH target genes in lingual progenitors at birth and show that SHH overexpression in vivo alters FoxA1 and FoxA2 expression relevant to taste buds.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Genes relevant to cell adhesion and cell locomotion are likely regulated by FOXA1;FOXA2.
source: We further bioinformatically identify genes relevant to cell adhesion and cell locomotion likely regulated by FOXA1;FOXA2 and show that expression of these candidates is also altered by forced SHH expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by motif analysis and GO term analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Expression of cell adhesion and cell locomotion genes is altered by forced SHH expression.
source: We further bioinformatically identify genes relevant to cell adhesion and cell locomotion likely regulated by FOXA1;FOXA2 and show that expression of these candidates is also altered by forced SHH expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: SHH promotes TRC differentiation by regulating changes in epithelial cell adhesion and migration.
source: We present a new model where SHH promotes TRC differentiation by regulating changes in epithelial cell adhesion and migration.
evidence: This is the proposed model of the study stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Taste buds reside in three types of specialized epithelial papillae on the tongue: fungiform (FFP) in the anterior tongue and circumvallate and foliate, posteriorly.
source: Taste buds are the primary end organs of the gustatory system, which reside in three types of specialized epithelial papillae on the tongue: fungiform (FFP) in the anterior tongue and circumvallate and foliate, posteriorly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about taste bud anatomy.

claim: Each taste bud houses a collection of heterogeneous taste receptor cells (TRCs) that transduce taste stimuli.
source: Regardless of papilla location, each taste bud houses a collection of heterogeneous taste receptor cells (TRCs) that transduce taste stimuli, including sweet, umami, salt, sour, and bitter, to signal palatability, nutritional value, and/or danger of substances in the oral cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about taste bud function.

claim: TRCs transduce taste stimuli including sweet, umami, salt, sour, and bitter.
source: Regardless of papilla location, each taste bud houses a collection of heterogeneous taste receptor cells (TRCs) that transduce taste stimuli, including sweet, umami, salt, sour, and bitter, to signal palatability, nutritional value, and/or danger of substances in the oral cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about taste modalities.

claim: Taste signals are conveyed from taste buds to the brain via gustatory nerve fibers of the VIIth and IXth cranial nerves.
source: These signals are conveyed from taste buds to the brain via gustatory nerve fibers of the VIIth and IXth cranial nerves.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about taste signal transmission.

claim: All TRCs are modified epithelial cells.
source: Despite some neuronal characteristics that accompany their sensory function, all TRCs are modified epithelial cells and are continuously renewed (see Barlow and Klein, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Adult taste cells are generated from progenitors adjacent to taste buds that express cytokeratin 14 (KRT14) and KRT5.
source: Adult taste cells are generated from progenitors adjacent to taste buds that express cytokeratin 14 (KRT14) and KRT5 (Gaillard et al., 2015; Okubo et al., 2009), a population of basal keratinocytes that also gives rise to the non-taste lingual epithelium that covers the tongue surface.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KRT14+ and KRT5+ basal keratinocytes give rise to both taste cells and non-taste lingual epithelium.
source: Adult taste cells are generated from progenitors adjacent to taste buds that express cytokeratin 14 (KRT14) and KRT5 (Gaillard et al., 2015; Okubo et al., 2009), a population of basal keratinocytes that also gives rise to the non-taste lingual epithelium that covers the tongue surface.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Taste-fated daughter cells exit the cell cycle and enter buds as post-mitotic taste precursor cells that express sonic hedgehog (SHH).
source: Taste-fated daughter cells exit the cell cycle, enter buds as post-mitotic taste precursor cells that express sonic hedgehog (SHH), and differentiate directly into functional TRCs (Miura et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Post-mitotic taste precursor cells differentiate directly into functional TRCs.
source: Taste-fated daughter cells exit the cell cycle, enter buds as post-mitotic taste precursor cells that express sonic hedgehog (SHH), and differentiate directly into functional TRCs (Miura et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Taste bud primordia first develop as focal epithelial thickenings, or taste placodes, on the mouse tongue at mid-gestation (embryonic day [E] 12.0).
source: Embryonically, taste bud primordia first develop as focal epithelial thickenings, or taste placodes, on the mouse tongue at mid-gestation (embryonic day [E] 12.0) (Mistretta and Bosma, 1972; Mistretta and Liu, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: In the anterior tongue, placodes undergo morphogenesis to form FFP.
source: In the anterior tongue, placodes undergo morphogenesis to form FFP, and taste bud primordia are first innervated by gustatory fibers at E14.5 (Lopez and Krimm, 2006); differentiated TRCs are observed in the first postnatal week (Ohtubo et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Taste bud primordia are first innervated by gustatory fibers at E14.5.
source: In the anterior tongue, placodes undergo morphogenesis to form FFP, and taste bud primordia are first innervated by gustatory fibers at E14.5 (Lopez and Krimm, 2006); differentiated TRCs are observed in the first postnatal week (Ohtubo et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Differentiated TRCs are observed in the first postnatal week.
source: In the anterior tongue, placodes undergo morphogenesis to form FFP, and taste bud primordia are first innervated by gustatory fibers at E14.5 (Lopez and Krimm, 2006); differentiated TRCs are observed in the first postnatal week (Ohtubo et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Shh and target genes Gli1 and Ptch1 are initially co-expressed broadly by lingual epithelium.
source: Shh and target genes Gli1 and Ptch1 are initially co-expressed broadly by lingual epithelium; at E12.5, this pattern resolves to placode-specific SHH expression as taste placodes are specified, while placode-adjacent epithelial cells remain Gli1+/Ptch1+ (Hall et al., 1999; Jung et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: At E12.5, SHH expression becomes placode-specific as taste placodes are specified.
source: Shh and target genes Gli1 and Ptch1 are initially co-expressed broadly by lingual epithelium; at E12.5, this pattern resolves to placode-specific SHH expression as taste placodes are specified, while placode-adjacent epithelial cells remain Gli1+/Ptch1+ (Hall et al., 1999; Jung et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Placode-adjacent epithelial cells remain Gli1+/Ptch1+ at E12.5.
source: Shh and target genes Gli1 and Ptch1 are initially co-expressed broadly by lingual epithelium; at E12.5, this pattern resolves to placode-specific SHH expression as taste placodes are specified, while placode-adjacent epithelial cells remain Gli1+/Ptch1+ (Hall et al., 1999; Jung et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Embryonic lineage tracing reveals SHH+ placode cells become the first differentiated TRCs after birth.
source: Embryonic lineage tracing reveals SHH+ placode cells become the first differentiated TRCs after birth (Thirumangalathu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: SHH+ placodes do not give rise to adult taste progenitors.
source: However, SHH+ placodes do not give rise to adult taste progenitors, as SHH-derived TRCs are steadily lost from taste buds within a few postnatal months (Thirumangalathu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: SHH-derived TRCs are steadily lost from taste buds within a few postnatal months.
source: However, SHH+ placodes do not give rise to adult taste progenitors, as SHH-derived TRCs are steadily lost from taste buds within a few postnatal months (Thirumangalathu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Lineage tracing of KRT14+ cells initiated in the first postnatal week labels small numbers of taste cells.
source: By contrast, lineage tracing of KRT14+ cells initiated in the first postnatal week labels small numbers of taste cells, suggesting that the adult progenitor population is activated in the days following birth (Okubo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The adult progenitor population is activated in the days following birth.
source: By contrast, lineage tracing of KRT14+ cells initiated in the first postnatal week labels small numbers of taste cells, suggesting that the adult progenitor population is activated in the days following birth (Okubo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: In embryos, SHH functions to repress taste fate as taste placodes are specified and patterned.
source: In embryos, SHH functions to repress taste fate as taste placodes are specified and patterned (El Shahawy et al., 2017; Hall et al., 2003; Iwatsuki et al., 2007; Mistretta et al., 2003); while once taste placodes are established, embryonic taste primordia no longer respond to pharmacological manipulation of hedgehog signaling (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Once taste placodes are established, embryonic taste primordia no longer respond to pharmacological manipulation of hedgehog signaling.
source: In embryos, SHH functions to repress taste fate as taste placodes are specified and patterned (El Shahawy et al., 2017; Hall et al., 2003; Iwatsuki et al., 2007; Mistretta et al., 2003); while once taste placodes are established, embryonic taste primordia no longer respond to pharmacological manipulation of hedgehog signaling (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: In adults, SHH promotes and is required for TRC differentiation.
source: By contrast, in adults, SHH promotes and is required for TRC differentiation. Specifically, ectopic expression of SHH drives formation of ectopic taste buds (Castillo et al., 2014), while pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of Hedgehog (Hh) pathway components leads to loss of taste buds (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017; Ermilov et al., 2016; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of SHH drives formation of ectopic taste buds in adults.
source: Specifically, ectopic expression of SHH drives formation of ectopic taste buds (Castillo et al., 2014), while pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of Hedgehog (Hh) pathway components leads to loss of taste buds (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017; Ermilov et al., 2016; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of Hedgehog (Hh) pathway components leads to loss of taste buds in adults.
source: Specifically, ectopic expression of SHH drives formation of ectopic taste buds (Castillo et al., 2014), while pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of Hedgehog (Hh) pathway components leads to loss of taste buds (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017; Ermilov et al., 2016; Kumari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: SOX2 is a key regulator of embryonic taste bud formation and adult taste cell renewal.
source: SOX2, an SRY-related HMG-box transcription factor, is also a key regulator of embryonic taste bud formation and adult taste cell renewal, and in both contexts, SOX2 is required for TRC differentiation (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2018; Ohmoto et al., 2020; Okubo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: SOX2 is required for TRC differentiation in both embryonic and adult contexts.
source: SOX2, an SRY-related HMG-box transcription factor, is also a key regulator of embryonic taste bud formation and adult taste cell renewal, and in both contexts, SOX2 is required for TRC differentiation (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2018; Ohmoto et al., 2020; Okubo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: SOX2 function is required downstream of SHH in adult taste cell homeostasis.
source: Additionally, SOX2 function is required downstream of SHH, at least in adult taste cell homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Before taste placodes emerge, the tongue anlage is covered by a simple bilayered epithelium that broadly expresses KRT8.
source: Before taste placodes emerge, the tongue anlage is covered by a simple bilayered epithelium that broadly expresses KRT8 (Mbiene and Roberts, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, supported by a citation and confirmed by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-C'.

claim: KRT14 is co-expressed with KRT8 throughout the lingual epithelium at E12.0.
source: We observed KRT14 co-expression with KRT8 throughout the lingual epithelium at E12.0 (Figure 1A–C').
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A-C'.

claim: At E13.5, following placode specification, KRT8 is expressed in placodes and downregulated in non-taste epithelium.
source: At E13.5, following placode specification, KRT8 is expressed in placodes and downregulated in non-taste epithelium, although, consistent with previous reports, KRT8 persists in superficial periderm (Figure 1D–F, yellow arrows in E) (Mbiene and Roberts, 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: At E13.5, KRT14 expression is mostly lost from placodes but evident in cells adjacent to placodes as well as throughout the lingual epithelium.
source: At E13.5, KRT14 expression is mostly lost from placodes but evident in cells adjacent to placodes as well as throughout the lingual epithelium.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: At E16.5, KRT8+ taste bud primordia are KRT14− immunonegative in each FFP.
source: These patterns are refined at E16.5; in each FFP, KRT8+ taste bud primordia are KRT14− immunonegative (Figure 1I, asterisk), and KRT8 expression is fully absent from KRT14+ non-taste lingual epithelium as the periderm is lost by this stage (Sengel, 1976; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: KRT8 expression is fully absent from KRT14+ non-taste lingual epithelium at E16.5 as the periderm is lost by this stage.
source: These patterns are refined at E16.5; in each FFP, KRT8+ taste bud primordia are KRT14− immunonegative (Figure 1I, asterisk), and KRT8 expression is fully absent from KRT14+ non-taste lingual epithelium as the periderm is lost by this stage (Sengel, 1976; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G-H and a citation.

claim: Taste placodes emerge from embryonic stratifying epithelium that co-expresses KRT14 and KRT8.
source: Thus, taste placodes emerge from embryonic stratifying epithelium that co-expresses KRT14 and KRT8; placode specification results in downregulation of placodal KRT14 and maintenance of KRT8 in taste bud primordia, while KRT14+ non-taste epithelium downregulates KRT8.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Placode specification results in downregulation of placodal KRT14 and maintenance of KRT8 in taste bud primordia.
source: Thus, taste placodes emerge from embryonic stratifying epithelium that co-expresses KRT14 and KRT8; placode specification results in downregulation of placodal KRT14 and maintenance of KRT8 in taste bud primordia, while KRT14+ non-taste epithelium downregulates KRT8.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: KRT14+ non-taste epithelium downregulates KRT8 following placode specification.
source: Thus, taste placodes emerge from embryonic stratifying epithelium that co-expresses KRT14 and KRT8; placode specification results in downregulation of placodal KRT14 and maintenance of KRT8 in taste bud primordia, while KRT14+ non-taste epithelium downregulates KRT8.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: When K14-tomato was induced at E12.5 and assayed 48 hr later (E14.5), most KRT8+ placodal cells were tomato+.
source: When K14-tomato was induced at E12.5 and assayed 48 hr later (E14.5), most KRT8+ placodal cells were tomato+ (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: KRT14-tomato lineage trace initiated at E14.5 resulted in 50% tomato+/KRT8+ cells 48 hr later (E16.5).
source: Despite limited KRT14 immunoreactivity in taste placodes at E13.5 (see Figure 1F), KRT14-tomato lineage trace initiated at E14.5 resulted in 50% tomato+/KRT8+ cells 48 hr later (E16.5. Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: At E17.5 after lineage trace induction at E15.5, most KRT8+ taste bud primordia fully lacked tomato+ cells.
source: At E17.5 after lineage trace induction at E15.5, most KRT8+ taste bud primordia fully lacked tomato+ cells (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Taste placodes are post-mitotic.
source: Taste placodes are post-mitotic (Farbman and Mbiene, 1991; Mbiene and Roberts, 2003; Thirumangalathu and Barlow, 2015); thus, if embryonic KRT14+ progenitors contribute new cells to placodes, the number of cells per placode should increase during development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Developing taste buds were static in both cell number and volume between E13.5 and E16.5.
source: We found developing taste buds were static in both cell number and volume (Figure 1P,Q), ruling out an embryonic KRT14+ progenitor contribution to taste bud primordia following placode specification.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1P,Q.

claim: Embryonic KRT14+ progenitors do not contribute to taste bud primordia following placode specification.
source: We found developing taste buds were static in both cell number and volume (Figure 1P,Q), ruling out an embryonic KRT14+ progenitor contribution to taste bud primordia following placode specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the cell number and volume data shown in Figure 1P,Q.

claim: KRT8+ taste cell number increased significantly between P2 and P9.
source: KRT8+ taste cell number was comparable between E16.5 and P2 but increased significantly between P2 and P9 (Figure 2A), suggestive of the addition of new taste cells during the first postnatal week.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In pups treated with EdU at P0, EdU+ cells were observed within KRT8+ taste buds 48 hr later.
source: In pups treated with 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) at P0, EdU+ cells were observed within KRT8+ taste buds 48 hr later, indicating the addition of new taste cells begins at birth (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by EdU birthdating data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The addition of new taste cells begins at birth.
source: In pups treated with 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) at P0, EdU+ cells were observed within KRT8+ taste buds 48 hr later, indicating the addition of new taste cells begins at birth (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the EdU birthdating data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Comparable rates of intragemmal labeling were observed in postnatal taste buds when EdU was administered at P7 or P14 and quantified at P9 or P16, respectively.
source: Comparable rates of intragemmal labeling were observed in postnatal taste buds when EdU was administered at P7 or P14 and quantified at P9 or P16, respectively (Figure 2B,D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by EdU birthdating data shown in Figure 2B,D,E.

claim: YFP+KRT8+ cells were readily observed within taste buds at P2, P9, and P16 following K14-YFP induction at P0, P7, or P14, respectively.
source: YFP+KRT8+ cells were readily observed within taste buds at each stage (Figure 2F–I); additionally, the proportion of taste buds with KRT14-lineage traced cells increased significantly over the first two postnatal weeks (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: The proportion of taste buds with KRT14-lineage traced cells increased significantly over the first two postnatal weeks.
source: YFP+KRT8+ cells were readily observed within taste buds at each stage (Figure 2F–I); additionally, the proportion of taste buds with KRT14-lineage traced cells increased significantly over the first two postnatal weeks (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: KRT14+ progenitors generate new taste cells at birth.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that KRT14+ progenitors generate new taste cells at birth, and this contribution steadily increases postnatally, leading to taste bud growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the EdU and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The contribution of KRT14+ progenitors to taste buds steadily increases postnatally, leading to taste bud growth.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that KRT14+ progenitors generate new taste cells at birth, and this contribution steadily increases postnatally, leading to taste bud growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the EdU and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Murine taste buds each house ~60 functionally and morphologically heterogeneous cells.
source: Murine taste buds each house ~60 functionally and morphologically heterogeneous cells, including type I support cells, type II detectors of sweet, bitter or umami, and type III sour receptor cells (Roper and Chaudhari, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: At 6 weeks, embryonically derived type I and type II TRCs were readily observed, but lineage labeled type III cells were not.
source: Previously, we used a low-efficiency Cre reporter to trace SHH-expressing taste placode cells from E12.5 into adulthood (ShhCreERT2;R26RLacZ) (Thirumangalathu et al., 2009). At 6 weeks, embryonically derived type I and type II TRCs were readily observed, but lineage labeled type III cells were not, suggesting embryonic taste precursors may be lineage restricted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a previous finding, supported by a citation.

claim: Type III cells account for <10% of adult TRCs.
source: However, type III cells account for <10% of adult TRCs (Ma et al., 2007; Ohtubo and Yoshii, 2011), and our previous experimental parameters were not optimized to detect this less common cell population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: ~70% of both NCAM+ cells and CAR4+ cells were tomato+ at P14 following SHH lineage tracing initiated at E12.5.
source: Immunostaining for type III TRC markers NCAM and CAR4 revealed significant double labeling in Shh-tomato taste buds. Specifically, ~70% of both NCAM+ cells and CAR4+ cells were tomato+ at P14 (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J-L.

claim: ~60% of PLCß2+ type II cells were tomato+ at P14, following placodal lineage trace initiated at E12.5.
source: Similarly, ~60% of PLCß2+ type II cells were tomato+ at P14, following placodal lineage trace initiated at E12.5 (Figure 2J,M).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J,M.

claim: SHH+ taste placode cells give rise to all TRC types postnatally.
source: Together with our previously published findings (Thirumangalathu et al., 2009), we show SHH+ taste placode cells give rise to all TRC types postnatally.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the lineage tracing and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Placodally derived cells comprise slight majorities of type II and III TRCs at P14.
source: Furthermore, we find placodally derived cells comprise slight majorities of type II and III TRCs at P14, suggesting that unlabeled TRCs were new cells derived from KRT14+ progenitors in the first postnatal weeks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the lineage tracing and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In adult rodents, type II and III TRCs require ~3.5 days from their terminal division to turn on expression of cell type-specific immunomarkers.
source: In adult rodents, type II and III TRCs require ~3.5 days from their terminal division to turn on expression of cell type-specific immunomarkers (Cho et al., 1998; Hamamichi et al., 2006; Perea-Martinez et al., 2013); the lack of double labeling in short -term postnatal lineage tracing here suggested the rate of differentiation of postnatally derived TRCs is comparable to that of adults.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: KRT14 lineage tracing resulted in labeling of both type II and III cells in comparable but not identical proportions to SHH lineage tracing.
source: Thus, we next examined the fate of newly generated TRCs in tongues from mice traced by induction of K14-YFP at P1 and harvested at P15. Similar to ShhCreERT2 lineage tracing, KRT14 lineage tracing resulted in labeling of both type II and III cells in comparable but not identical proportions (Figure 2N–Q), indicating that SHH+ taste primordia and postnatal KRT14+ progenitors, nonetheless, have no bias in terms of taste cell type production and are both competent to differentiate the full taste bud lineage.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2N-Q.

claim: SHH+ taste primordia and postnatal KRT14+ progenitors have no bias in terms of taste cell type production and are both competent to differentiate the full taste bud lineage.
source: Thus, we next examined the fate of newly generated TRCs in tongues from mice traced by induction of K14-YFP at P1 and harvested at P15. Similar to ShhCreERT2 lineage tracing, KRT14 lineage tracing resulted in labeling of both type II and III cells in comparable but not identical proportions (Figure 2N–Q), indicating that SHH+ taste primordia and postnatal KRT14+ progenitors, nonetheless, have no bias in terms of taste cell type production and are both competent to differentiate the full taste bud lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the lineage tracing and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2N-Q.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic deletion of SHH signaling during placode specification results in overproduction of enlarged taste buds.
source: Pharmacologic inhibition or genetic deletion of SHH signaling during placode specification results in overproduction of enlarged taste buds (El Shahawy et al., 2017; Hall et al., 2003; Iwatsuki et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2004; Mistretta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Differentiated type I and II TRCs are present within a subset of taste buds at E18.5.
source: Previously, we observed differentiated type I and II TRCs within a subset of taste buds at E18.5 (Thirumangalathu and Barlow, 2015), and further analysis here reveals differentiation of all three TRC types is underway at E17.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a previous finding, supported by a citation and confirmed by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differentiation of all three TRC types is underway at E17.5.
source: Previously, we observed differentiated type I and II TRCs within a subset of taste buds at E18.5 (Thirumangalathu and Barlow, 2015), and further analysis here reveals differentiation of all three TRC types is underway at E17.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tamoxifen induction at E13.5 in ShhCreERT2/fl mice resulted in reduced Shh mRNA in E18.5 lingual epithelium, as well as reduced expression of Gli1.
source: Tamoxifen induction at E13.5 resulted in reduced Shh mRNA in E18.5 lingual epithelium, as well as reduced expression of its target transcriptional regulator, Gli1 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Shh-ShhcKO embryos induced at E12.5 and analyzed E18.5, the total number and size of KRT8+ taste buds and FFP were significantly increased.
source: In Shh-ShhcKO embyos induced at E12.5 and analyzed E18.5, the total number and size of KRT8+ taste buds and FFP were significantly increased (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B-F.

claim: E12.5 Shh-ShhcKO significantly increased the proportion of taste buds containing differentiated type I (NTPdase2+), II (PLCß2+), and III (NCAM+) TRCs compared to Shhwt/fl littermate controls.
source: Additionally, E12.5 Shh-ShhcKO significantly increased the proportion of taste buds containing differentiated type I (NTPdase2+), II (PLCß2+), and III (NCAM+) TRCs compared to Shhwt/fl littermate controls (Figure 3G–I), indicating that Shh reduction during placode specification accelerated taste bud differentiation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Shh reduction during placode specification accelerated taste bud differentiation.
source: Additionally, E12.5 Shh-ShhcKO significantly increased the proportion of taste buds containing differentiated type I (NTPdase2+), II (PLCß2+), and III (NCAM+) TRCs compared to Shhwt/fl littermate controls (Figure 3G–I), indicating that Shh reduction during placode specification accelerated taste bud differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: The acceleration of TRC differentiation by early SHH deletion is likely due to the loss of Shh's repressive role on Wnt/ß-catenin signaling during placode specification.
source: This outcome is likely due to the loss of Shh's repressive role on Wnt/ß-catenin signaling during placode specification that in turn leads to precocious TRC differentiation (Iwatsuki et al., 2007; Thirumangalathu and Barlow, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section, based on the current findings and previous studies cited.

claim: ShhcKO induced at E16.5 did not alter the number or size of FFP or KRT8+ taste buds.
source: Consistent with this, ShhcKO induced at E16.5 did not alter the number or size of FFP or KRT8+ taste buds (Figure 3B,J,K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B,J,K.

claim: E16.5 induction of ShhcKO did not accelerate TRC differentiation.
source: Moreover, E16.5 induction of ShhcKO did not accelerate TRC differentiation; similar proportions of taste buds housed type I (NTPdase2+), II (PLCß2+), and III (NCAM+) TRCs in ShhcKO and control tongues at E20 (Figure 3L-N).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: Taste epithelium is not sensitive to Shh pathway inhibition in late gestation.
source: Our in vivo results confirm and expand upon in vitro studies showing taste epithelium is not sensitive to Shh pathway inhibition in late gestation (Liu et al., 2004) (but see Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the current findings and previous studies cited.

claim: In adult lingual epithelium misexpression of SHH induces ectopic taste buds in non-taste lingual epithelium.
source: In contrast to its repressive function in embryos, in adult lingual epithelium misexpression of SHH induces ectopic taste buds in non-taste lingual epithelium (Castillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: When K14-SHHcKI was induced at P1 and assessed at P15, small numbers of ectopic KRT8+ cells were detected in SHH-YFP+ non-taste lingual epithelium.
source: When K14-SHHcKI was induced at P1 and assessed at P15, small numbers of ectopic KRT8+ cells were detected in SHH-YFP+ non-taste lingual epithelium (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Significantly more KRT8+ cell clusters formed in K14-SHHcKI tongues induced at P14 and harvested at P28.
source: Significantly more KRT8+ cell clusters formed in K14-SHHcKI tongues induced at P14 and harvested at P28 (Figure 3C,D), and these ectopic buds co-expressed markers of type I (NTPdase2), II (PLCß2), and III TRCs (5HT; Huang et al., 2005; Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Ectopic taste buds induced by postnatal SHH overexpression co-expressed markers of type I (NTPdase2), II (PLCß2), and III TRCs (5HT).
source: Significantly more KRT8+ cell clusters formed in K14-SHHcKI tongues induced at P14 and harvested at P28 (Figure 3C,D), and these ectopic buds co-expressed markers of type I (NTPdase2), II (PLCß2), and III TRCs (5HT; Huang et al., 2005; Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Forced SHH expression postnatally had no effect on endogenous FFP taste bud number.
source: Notably, forced SHH expression postnatally had no effect on endogenous FFP taste bud number (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: Embryonic induction of K14-SHHcKI at E12.5 did not lead to the formation of ectopic buds at P14, but repressed endogenous FFP taste bud development.
source: By contrast, embryonic induction of K14-SHHcKI at E12.5 did not lead to the formation of ectopic buds at P14, but as expected repressed endogenous FFP taste bud development (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In adult tongue, SHH is expressed by gustatory sensory neurons of the VIIth cranial ganglion as well as post-mitotic taste precursor cells.
source: In adult tongue, SHH is expressed by gustatory sensory neurons of the VIIth cranial ganglion as well as post-mitotic taste precursor cells that differentiate all three functional TRCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: Gustatory neurons and taste precursor cells together supply SHH to support continual TRC differentiation.
source: We have shown these cell populations together supply SHH to support continual TRC differentiation (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017; Miura et al., 2003; but see Lu et al., 2018 and discussed below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a previous finding, supported by citations.

claim: Embryonic taste placodes are not innervated at specification, hence the only early source of lingual SHH is placodal.
source: However, embryonic taste placodes are not innervated at specification, hence the only early source of lingual SHH is placodal (Hall et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Gustatory neurons develop by E10.5.
source: Gustatory neurons develop by E10.5 (Cordes, 2001) and gustatory neurites first penetrate the taste epithelium at E14.5 (Krimm, 2007; Lopez and Krimm, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Gustatory neurites first penetrate the taste epithelium at E14.5.
source: Gustatory neurons develop by E10.5 (Cordes, 2001) and gustatory neurites first penetrate the taste epithelium at E14.5 (Krimm, 2007; Lopez and Krimm, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Shh lineage tracing initiated at E12.5 revealed that ~1/3rd of taste buds were contacted by one or more tomato+ neurites at P14.
source: Thus, we induced Shh-tomato lineage tracing in embryos during placode specification (E12.5) and quantified the number of tomato+ nerve fibers within the core of each FFP at P14. In addition to ample taste bud cell labeling as expected, Shh lineage tracing revealed that ~1/3rd of taste buds were contacted by one or more tomato+ neurites at P14 (Figure 5A,C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5A,C,D.

claim: Some gustatory neurons already express SHH as early as E12.5.
source: Thus, some gustatory neurons already express SHH as early as E12.5.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5A,C,D.

claim: When lineage tracing was induced at birth (P0) and examined at P14, the proportion of FFP with tomato+ neurites increased significantly and taste buds were contacted by more tomato+ neurites.
source: When lineage tracing was induced at birth (P0), well after nerve contacts are established, and similarly examined at P14, the proportion of FFP with tomato+ neurites increased significantly and taste buds were contacted by more tomato+ neurites (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Some gustatory neurons express SHH embryonically, well before the shift in SHH function, which occurs at birth.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that some gustatory neurons express SHH embryonically, well before the shift in SHH function, which occurs at birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Taste bud size and number do not differ between controls and Phox2b-SHHcKO mice at 10 weeks postnatal.
source: When assessed at 10 weeks, taste buds in Phox2b-ShhcKO mice were indistinguishable from control Phox2bCre; R26RtdTomato littermates; we found no differences in taste bud number, size (KRT8+ pixels/taste bud), or type II or III TRC differentiation (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: Phox2b-ShhcKO does not disrupt differentiation of PLCß2+ type II or SNAP25+ type III taste cells.
source: When assessed at 10 weeks, taste buds in Phox2b-ShhcKO mice were indistinguishable from control Phox2bCre; R26RtdTomato littermates; we found no differences in taste bud number, size (KRT8+ pixels/taste bud), or type II or III TRC differentiation (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5I-J.

claim: Neural SHH is dispensable for embryonic taste placode specification and postnatal taste bud differentiation.
source: These results suggest that neural SHH is dispensable for embryonic taste placode specification and postnatal taste bud differentiation, and are consistent with our previously findings in adults where epithelial SHH can compensate for loss of neuronal SHH to maintain adult taste buds (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the Phox2b-ShhcKO data shown in Figure 5 and previous findings cited.

claim: Epithelial SHH can compensate for loss of neuronal SHH to maintain adult taste buds.
source: These results suggest that neural SHH is dispensable for embryonic taste placode specification and postnatal taste bud differentiation, and are consistent with our previously findings in adults where epithelial SHH can compensate for loss of neuronal SHH to maintain adult taste buds (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a previous finding, supported by a citation.

claim: SOX2 plays a critical role in taste bud development and renewal and is required downstream of SHH for adult taste bud differentiation.
source: The transcription factor SOX2 plays a critical role in taste bud development and renewal and is required downstream of SHH for adult taste bud differentiation (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2018; Ohmoto et al., 2020; Okubo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: At P0, SOX2 is highly expressed in and around KRT8+ taste buds, moderately expressed by FFP basal progenitors, and dimly expressed by basal keratinocytes of the interpapilliary non-taste epithelium.
source: At P0, SOX2 is highly expressed in and around KRT8+ taste buds (Figure 6A, yellow arrows), moderately expressed by FFP basal progenitors (Figure 6A, yellow arrowheads), and dimly expressed by basal keratinocytes of the interpapilliary non-taste epithelium (Figure 6A, white arrowheads; see Nakayama et al., 2015), an expression pattern that is recapitulated in SOX2-EGFP (SOX2-GFP) reporter mice (Figure 6B; Okubo et al., 2006; Taranova et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,B and citations.

claim: High SOX2 is associated with taste fate, while moderate/dim SOX2 marks non-taste progenitors.
source: This expression pattern has led to the suggestion that high SOX2 is associated with taste fate, while moderate/dim SOX2 marks non-taste progenitors (Castillo-Azofeifa et al., 2018; Nakayama et al., 2015; Okubo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Sox2 was expressed 2× higher in GFPhigh cells compared to GFPlow cells by qPCR.
source: Confirming the efficacy of cell sorting, Sox2 was expressed 2× higher in GFPhigh cells compared to GFPlow cells by qPCR (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Using a 5 FPKM threshold and enrichment of 1.5-fold or greater expression over the opposing population, 1032 GFPhigh and 970 GFPlow DEGs were identified.
source: Using a 5 FPKM threshold and enrichment of 1.5-fold or greater expression over the opposing population, we identified 1032 GFPhigh and 970 GFPlow DEGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 1b, 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary files.

claim: Taste and progenitor-associated genes were enriched in GFPhigh cells, including Slc6a11, Shh, Prox1, Lrmp, Ptch2, Slc6a13, Lgr5, Rarb, Six1, Bdnf, Wnt10b, Krt8, Krt19, Krt7, and Hes6.
source: As expected, taste and progenitor-associated genes were enriched in GFPhigh cells, including Slc6a11, Shh, Prox1, Lrmp, Ptch2, Slc6a13, Lgr5, Rarb, Six1, Bdnf, Wnt10b, Krt8, Krt19, Krt7, and Hes6 (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: GFPlow DEGs included markers of both epithelium (Lyg1, Krtap3-1, Krt84, Krt36, Krt83, Krtap13-1, Gfra2, Itga8, Krt81) and connective tissue (Foxd3, Sox10, Mpz, Ednrb, Zeb2, Cdh6).
source: By contrast, GFPlow DEGs included markers of both epithelium (Lyg1, Krtap3-1, Krt84, Krt36, Krt83, Krtap13-1, Gfra2, Itga8, Krt81) and connective tissue (Foxd3, Sox10, Mpz, Ednrb, Zeb2, Cdh6) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: SOX2-GFPhigh cells comprise an epithelial taste/progenitor enriched population, while SOX2-GFPlow cells represent a mixed population of lingual epithelium and connective tissue.
source: Thus, SOX2-GFPhigh cells comprise an epithelial taste/progenitor enriched population, while SOX2-GFPlow cells represent a mixed population of lingual epithelium and connective tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the RNAseq and GO analysis data shown in Figure 6 and Supplementary files.

claim: Hh pathway components were expressed by both GFPhigh and GFPlow cells.
source: As expected, Hh pathway components were expressed by both GFPhigh and GFPlow cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Shh, Ptch1, and Gli1 were enriched in GFPhigh compared to GFPlow cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports, Shh, Ptch1, and Gli1 were enriched in GFPhigh compared to GFPlow cells (Figure 6G,I; Hall et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq and qPCR data shown in Figure 6G,I and citations.

claim: The transmembrane receptor Ptch2 was highly enriched in the GFPhigh population.
source: Additionally, the transmembrane receptor Ptch2 was highly enriched in the GFPhigh population, while Hh-interacting protein Hhip was highly enriched in GFPlow cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data.

claim: Hh-interacting protein Hhip was highly enriched in GFPlow cells.
source: Additionally, the transmembrane receptor Ptch2 was highly enriched in the GFPhigh population, while Hh-interacting protein Hhip was highly enriched in GFPlow cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data.

claim: Of the 201 transcription factors identified by AME, only 123 were expressed within the P0 dataset.
source: Of the 201 transcription factors identified by AME, only 123 were expressed within our P0 dataset (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by motif enrichment analysis data in Supplementary file 1f.

claim: ~20% of the 123 expressed transcription factors were associated directly or indirectly with the SHH pathway, including Sox2, FoxA1, and FoxA2.
source: A literature search revealed ~20% of these candidates were associated directly or indirectly with the SHH pathway, including Sox2, FoxA1, and FoxA2.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section, based on motif enrichment analysis and literature search.

claim: Sox2 and Foxa2 were enriched within the GFPhigh population (1.9× and 2.6×, respectively), while Foxa1 was enriched in GFPlow cells (−5.65×).
source: In our dataset, Sox2 and Foxa2 were enriched within the GFPhigh population (1.9× and 2.6×, respectively), while Foxa1 was enriched in GFPlow cells (−5.65×) (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: Foxd3, a canonical mesenchyme gene, was expressed exclusively in GFPlow cells.
source: Notably, Foxd3, a canonical mesenchyme gene, was expressed exclusively in GFPlow cells (Figure 6H,J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by RNAseq and qPCR data shown in Figure 6H,J.

claim: FOXA2 and FOXA1 are broadly expressed in developing lingual epithelium at E13.5–15.5.
source: From published reports, FOXA2 and FOXA1 are broadly expressed in developing lingual epithelium at E13.5–15.5, and FOXA1 maintains broad expression at E18.5; by contrast, at E18.5, FOXA2 expression is absent from the general tongue epithelium and restricted to subsets of cells within taste buds and to clusters of keratinocytes at the base of FFP (Besnard et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge from published reports, supported by citations.

claim: At E18.5, FOXA2 expression is absent from the general tongue epithelium and restricted to subsets of cells within taste buds and to clusters of keratinocytes at the base of FFP.
source: From published reports, FOXA2 and FOXA1 are broadly expressed in developing lingual epithelium at E13.5–15.5, and FOXA1 maintains broad expression at E18.5; by contrast, at E18.5, FOXA2 expression is absent from the general tongue epithelium and restricted to subsets of cells within taste buds and to clusters of keratinocytes at the base of FFP (Besnard et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge from published reports, supported by citations.

claim: At E13.5, SOX2 is more highly expressed in KRT8+ taste placodes than by surrounding non-taste epithelium.
source: At E13.5, SOX2 is more highly expressed in KRT8+ taste placodes than by surrounding non-taste epithelium (Nakayama et al., 2015; Okubo et al., 2006; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, asterisk and arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: FOXA2 and FOXA1 are both expressed broadly by taste placode and non-taste epithelium at E13.5.
source: FOXA2 and FOXA1 are both expressed broadly by taste placode and non-taste epithelium (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C. placode: asterisk, non-taste epithelium: arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: At E16.5, FOXA2 expression is most intense in KRT8+ taste cells, moderate at the base of each FFP, and dim in non-taste epithelium; FOXA2 expression is absent from perigemmal cells.
source: At E16.5, FOXA2 expression has altered, and is most intense in KRT8+ taste cells, moderate at the base of each FFP, and dim in non-taste epithelium (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, white arrows and arrowheads); FOXA2 expression is absent from perigemmal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: FOXA1 expression at E16.5 is evident at low levels in sparse taste cells, absent in perigemmal cells, but robust in the developing filiform papilla and interpapillary non-taste epithelium.
source: FOXA1 expression at E16.5 has also shifted and is evident at low levels in sparse taste cells, absent in perigemmal cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F, yellow arrowheads), but robust in the developing filiform papilla and interpapillary non-taste epithelium (fi, ip).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Changes in expression of SOX2, FOXA2, and FOXA1 could contribute to the transformation of the lingual epithelial response to SHH from an embryonic repressor to a taste fate promoter in adults.
source: We conjecture that changes in expression of these three transcription factors could contribute to the transformation of the lingual epithelial response to SHH from an embryonic repressor to a taste fate promoter in adults.
evidence: This is a conjecture stated in the Results section, based on the expression pattern data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Induction of K14-SHHcKI in adult lingual epithelium leads to formation of ectopic taste buds, including induction of high SOX2 within and moderate SOX2 expression around ectopic buds.
source: Induction of K14-SHHcKI in adult lingual epithelium leads to formation of ectopic taste buds, including induction of high SOX2 within and moderate SOX2 expression around ectopic buds (Castillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR of Shh and Gli1 revealed Hh signaling was highly elevated in K14-SHHcKI tongues compared to controls, as was Sox2.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR of Shh and Gli1 revealed Hh signaling was highly elevated in K14-SHHcKI tongues compared to controls, as was Sox2 (Figure 7A), as expected.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Foxa2 was highly upregulated by K14-ShhcKI.
source: Likewise, Foxa2 was highly upregulated by K14-ShhcKI.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Foxa1 was significantly reduced by SHH overexpression.
source: However, Foxa1 was significantly reduced by SHH overexpression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: P0 induction of K14-SHHcKI led to ectopic FOXA2 expression at P15.
source: Similarly, P0 induction of K14-SHHcKI at P0 led to ectopic FOXA2 expression at P15. Within YFPneg 'control' domains, FOXA2 was strongly expressed by KRT8+ taste buds and entirely absent from non-taste epithelium (Figure 7D). In contrast, FOXA2 expression was increased in and around induced SHH-YFP+ cell patches, including within ectopic KRT8+ taste cells (Figure 7D–D", yellow arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D-D".

claim: Within the SOX2-GFPhigh dataset, 45.6% of DEG ROIs contained a SOX2 binding motif, 38.4% a FOXA2 motif, and 24.8% a FOXA1 motif.
source: Within the SOX2-GFPhigh dataset, 45.6% of DEG ROIs contained a SOX2 binding motif, 38.4% a FOXA2 motif, and 24.8% a FOXA1 motif; 143 DEG ROIs contained motifs of all three transcription factors, while 90 DEGs had motifs for SOX2 and FOXA2, 102 DEGs had motifs for FOXA1 and FOXA2, and only 6 DEGs had motifs for SOX2 and FOXA1 (Figure 8A Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 8A and Supplementary file 1g.

claim: FOXA2;FOXA1 DEGs were strongly enriched for terms including Regulation of cell adhesion and Positive regulation of cell migration.
source: However, FOXA2;FOXA1 DEGs were strongly enriched for terms including Regulation of cell adhesion and Positive regulation of cell migration (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by GO analysis data in Supplementary file 1i.

claim: Among genes common to both GO terms (Regulation of cell adhesion and Positive regulation of cell migration) were Pdpn (Podoplanin), Plet1 (Placenta expressed transcript 1), Cxcl10, and Tgfb2.
source: Among genes common to both GO terms were Pdpn (Podoplanin), Plet1 (Placenta expressed transcript 1), Cxcl10, and Tgfb2, while Runx1, Fbln2 (Fibulin 2), and Ephb4 were unique to Cell adhesion.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by GO analysis data.

claim: Runx1, Fbln2 (Fibulin 2), and Ephb4 were unique to the Cell adhesion GO term.
source: Among genes common to both GO terms were Pdpn (Podoplanin), Plet1 (Placenta expressed transcript 1), Cxcl10, and Tgfb2, while Runx1, Fbln2 (Fibulin 2), and Ephb4 were unique to Cell adhesion.
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by GO analysis data.

claim: Expression of cell adhesion genes (Runx1, Ephb4, and Fbln2) were significantly increased in response to SHH.
source: We found expression of cell adhesion genes (Runx1, Ephb4, and Fbln2) were significantly increased in response to SHH (Figure 8B), as were genes common to both GO terms (Plet1, Pdpn, and Cxcl10) although only the increase in Plet1 was significant (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Plet1 expression was significantly increased in response to SHH.
source: We found expression of cell adhesion genes (Runx1, Ephb4, and Fbln2) were significantly increased in response to SHH (Figure 8B), as were genes common to both GO terms (Plet1, Pdpn, and Cxcl10) although only the increase in Plet1 was significant (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tgfb2 was significantly reduced by SHH.
source: By contrast, Tgfb2 was significantly reduced by SHH (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study stated in the Results section and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: SHH promotes TRC differentiation via regulation of FOXA1 and FOXA2, which in turn regulate genes involved in cell adhesion and cell movement.
source: These data support a model where SHH promotes TRC differentiation via regulation of FOXA1 and FOXA2, which in turn regulate genes involved in cell adhesion and cell movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study stated in the Results section, based on the RNAseq, motif analysis, GO analysis, and qPCR data shown in Figures 6-8.
